- When sentiment is bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 2–5% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.  
- If recent events show high bearish net supply (e.g., net < -15) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast slope by 10–20% to avoid overestimating rebound.  
- After a sharp spike in true outcome (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots — cap forecast increase to 3–5% per day to avoid overcorrection.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated bullish spikes (e.g., 3+ consecutive 1.00s), model should not forecast a flat trend — expect mean reversion within 5–7 days unless policy changes.  
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low (≤0.33), forecast should be conservative — avoid upward drift; consider 1–2% downward bias to reflect supply constraints.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome shows early volatility (e.g., first 5 days > 70), model should not assume linear trend — add 1–2% downward correction to avoid overestimating peak.  
- If sentiment history shows mixed or neutral (0.00–0.50), forecast should be anchored to recent 7-day mean — avoid extrapolating from 18-day history.  
- When official events are high (e.g., >20 events/30d) and supply net is negative, forecast should be adjusted downward by 3–5% to reflect event-driven supply pressure.
